rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.2 <U+2014> three-year (2011-2013) split-plot field experiment with four replications at Kruszyn Krajenski, central Poland, on very light soil, factors drip irrigation (control vs drip) and N fertilization method (broadcasting vs drip fertigation). Q2: Section 3.2, Tables 6 and 8 <U+2014> nitrogen fertigation on average over the years significantly increased marketable tuber yield from 28.85 to 32.28 t/ha (about 12%) and tuber number per plant from 10.3 to 12.8 compared with broadcasting; highest yield in D + F (40.47 t/ha).
rows.notes: Single-method field trial (plot yield and tuber counts) at one site, one soil, one cultivar; no second independent method. Tuber weight and number are measured as yield components and a yield-tuber weight correlation is given (r = 0.912), but the mechanism by which fertigation raises yield (nutrient availability/uptake in the wet zone) is only asserted from literature, so Q4 is 'no'. Soil matric potential was monitored with tensiometers only to schedule irrigation. No support factor for the fertigation effect is stated as a requirement from own findings (light-soil effectiveness is cited, not derived). No limitations of the study are stated. Results given with Tukey letter groupings and p < 0.05 only; no SD, SE, CI or range reported for the fertigation effect. The 11.8% and 24.2% figures in the passage correspond closely to the study's 12% and 10.3-to-12.8 tubers (24.3%).

notes: Full text available; some tables are duplicated/garbled by layout in the extracted text but values are readable. Study is a conventional field experiment with no stated limitations and no dispersion statistics.
